rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 and 3.2 - the authors collected 715 face-to-face questionnaires from cotton farmers in nine counties/cities of Xinjiang and estimated a triple-hurdle model (Table 3) of adoption willingness, adoption decision and waiting time.
rows.notes: The study is a primary farm-household survey, but it does not test app-based scheduling or smart irrigation: the 'water-saving technology' studied is predominantly low-pressure pipe irrigation (Section 1, >90% of cotton farmers), and the outcome variables are farmers' willingness, decision and waiting time to adopt it as a function of capital endowment, land transfer, subsidies, neighbour adoption and cooperative membership. No effect of the technology on climate-risk management, resilience or yield stability is measured; adaptation is asserted in the framing only. The study at most shows determinants of adoption, which is a precondition of the claimed adaptive effect, and for a different technology than app scheduling. Limitations (cross-sectional data, omitted indicator) and standard errors in Table 3 relate to the adoption models, not to the claimed effect, so they do not count.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a socio-economic adoption analysis of water-saving irrigation technology (mainly low-pressure pipe irrigation) in Xinjiang; it contains no biophysical measurement of any irrigation technology's effect.
